record.original_question: (M. Larsen, A. Shalev, P. H. Tiep). A permutation on a set Ω is called a derangement if it has no fixed points in Ω. Let G be a finite simple transitive permutation group. Is it true that every element in G is the product of two derangements?

evidence.quote: (M. Larsen, A. Shalev, P. H. Tiep). A permutation on a set Ω is called a derangement if it has no fixed points in Ω. Let G be a finite simple transitive permutation group. Is it true that every element in G is the product of two derangements?

artifact.self_contained_problem: A permutation of a set $\Omega$ is called a derangement if it has no fixed points in $\Omega$. Let $G$ be a finite nonabelian simple group acting faithfully and transitively on a finite set $\Omega$. Determine whether every element of $G$ can be written as a product of two derangements in this action; equivalently, whether $G = \Delta(G)\cdot \Delta(G)$, where $\Delta(G) \subseteq G$ denotes the set of derangements of the action of $G$ on $\Omega$.
artifact.category_tag: derangements in finite simple permutation groups
artifact.status_search_result: Larsen, Shalev and Tiep (Forum of Math. Sigma, 2022) proved the conjecture for alternating groups and for sufficiently large finite simple transitive permutation groups, and explicitly conjecture that $G=\Delta(G)^2$ holds for every finite simple transitive group. Subsequent work (Burness–Guralnick et al., arXiv:2409.01043) establishes related results, such as generation by two conjugate derangements, and confirms $G=\Delta(G)^2$ for further classes, but the full conjecture remains open in general.

status_evidence.title: Products of derangements in simple permutation groups
status_evidence.snippet: Any element in a sufficiently large transitive finite simple permutation group is a product of two derangements; full conjecture stated.
status_evidence.claim: Result is proved for sufficiently large finite simple transitive permutation groups and conjectured in full generality.

status_evidence.title: On derangements in simple permutation groups
status_evidence.snippet: Every finite simple transitive group can be generated by two conjugate derangements; partial progress toward G=Δ(G)^2.
status_evidence.claim: Subsequent work extends partial results but does not fully resolve the conjecture.
